fatal_errors: The proposed Cu coating plus compression-plasma-flow treatment does not reconstruct the target intervention of liquid-metal dealloying a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.
The cited evidence concerns near-surface modification and metastable W(Cu) formation, not fabrication of a bulk, bicontinuous W–Cu heat-transfer composite.
Improved bulk thermal conductivity and mechanical durability under irradiation are asserted without direct supporting evidence from the cited study.
The stated 25–35 J/cm² processing range does not match the cited demonstrated range of 35–55 J/cm².
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the general W–Cu immiscibility, porosity, heat-transfer, and irradiation problem and proposes a scientifically plausible nonequilibrium alternative. Its mechanism of rapid surface melting and quench-assisted metastable W(Cu) formation is partly supported by the cited CPF work. However, it misses all defining features of the hidden target: the directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor, selective removal of Ti-rich channels by 1200 °C/96 h liquid-metal dealloying, retention of a continuous refractory-HEA network, formation of aligned Cu channels and a W-rich passivating interlayer, and the reported temperature-dependent thermal and He-implantation outcomes. The evidence does not establish that a shallow CPF-modified layer can eliminate defects throughout a macroscopic joint or improve its bulk conductivity, tensile strength, fracture resistance, or irradiation durability. The proposed controlled comparison has useful microscopy, diffraction, thermal, and mechanical endpoints, but it needs matched composition and density, quantified coating thickness and modified-layer depth, direct irradiation protocols, and separate criteria for each claimed outcome. Its arbitrary 20% void threshold does not by itself test the proposed solid-solution mechanism.
